title: How to Read a Cannabis Label | The Bridge
h1: How to Read a Cannabis Label
description: A New York cannabis label in plain language: the universal symbol, milligrams versus percent, the QR code and lab report, and what to check first.
lede: Most people read the strain name and the price, then stop. The part that actually answers your questions is printed on the back.
html:
Flip the package over before you fall for the name. The front is there to sell you something. The back is what New York makes a company stand behind, and it answers most of the questions people bring to the counter.

Start with the symbol, then check the store

Every regulated adult-use product in the state carries the New York universal symbol, which marks it as tested and regulated and tells you at a glance that it contains THC. One catch: the Office of Cannabis Management warns that some unregulated products copy the symbol. So the symbol only means something alongside the storefront. Licensed dispensaries post a Dispensary Verification Tool, and its QR code takes you to the state's list of licensed shops. The state tells buyers to check both.

Milligrams or percent

The number you are looking for changes with how the product enters your body.

  • Edibles, chews and lozenges list cannabinoids in milligrams, per serving and for the whole container. Read both. A New York edible may hold up to 10 milligrams of THC per serving, and a package can hold more than one serving.
  • Flower and pre-rolls list the percentage of the product made up of each cannabinoid, and usually name the cultivar, the state's word for strain.

Then comes the figure that confuses everyone. Lab paperwork can show THC, THCA and Total THC side by side. New York's law defines Total THC as the THC measured plus the THCA measured multiplied by 0.877. THCA is the form the plant mostly makes, and heat turns it into THC, so Total THC is the figure to read on flower. Say a report shows 1% THC and 25% THCA: 25 times 0.877, plus 1, comes to about 23%.

A big number is not a quality score. The state says so itself: a higher THC percentage does not mean a better experience, because terpenes and other cannabinoids shape it too.

Scan the code

All regulated products carry a QR code or link to a Certificate of Analysis, the lab report for that product. New York requires testing for cannabinoid profile, microorganisms, heavy metals, pesticides, residual solvents, water activity and foreign materials, among other contaminants. Two minutes with that page will tell you more than any menu description.

It has a limit. Cannabis changes when it is exposed to air, so a Certificate of Analysis won't stay accurate forever. The state's advice is to look at the expiration date, as long as you haven't opened the product since you bought it.

Compare all that with a package from an unlicensed seller. In the state's words, you can't trust any of the information on that label. It may not be lab tested, even if it says it is.

The warnings and the storage line

People skip this part, and they shouldn't. Labels carry warnings meant to prevent accidental consumption, the Poison Center number, and directions for use and storage. The state wants products kept in the original child-resistant package, and there is a practical reason beyond the kids: the Department of Health points out that the label tells emergency providers how much THC is in the product. If somebody you love ever eats the wrong thing, that package goes with you to the phone. The number is 1-800-222-1222.

Thirty seconds at the counter

  1. Symbol on the package, verification tool at the storefront.
  2. Milligrams per serving and servings per package, or Total THC and the cultivar.
  3. QR code: open it and read the results.
  4. Expiration date and storage directions.

Want the plant basics behind these numbers? Know Your Cannabis has them, and the shop is a good place to practice.
